newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWEDES STUDY IF MOBILE PHONES HARM USERS' HEALTH.
newsitem.headline: SWEDES STUDY IF MOBILE PHONES HARM USERS' HEALTH.

text.p: The world's widest investigation into the possibly harmful effects of mobile phones has begun in Norway and Sweden, its team leader said on Tuesday.

Twelve thousand people in Sweden, which has one of the world's highest per capita use of mobile phones, and 5,000 Norwegians will take part in the survey, partly funded by the mobile telephone industry.

Project leader Professor Kjell Hansson Mild, of Sweden's National Institute for Working Life, said many users of mobile phones had complained of headaches, a feeling of warmth or tingling in the face and head, dizziness and drowsiness.
Other complaints included nausea, memory loss and lack of concentration, he told Reuters by telephone from the institute at Umea in northern Sweden.
"These reports have appeared mainly in Sweden, the rest of Scandinavia, Australia, the United States and Britain," Hansson Mild said. "It is now time that we thoroughly investigate."
Sweden had been chosen because with about two million subscribers it was a country with one of the highest concentrations of mobile phones.
Sweden's registration procedures and other conditions woulod help guaranteed reliable results, he said.
Because Sweden has enthusiastically embraced the mobile phone, it may also have the best caseload of potential victims.
"We are looking at the heavy users of phones rather than people who make one call per day," Hansson Mild said.
"Lifestyle make also play a role, such as the level of stress and the individual personality."
Previous studies, though more narrowly based, have failed to prove any definitive link between the use of mobiles and ill-health.

However, some manufacturers have recommended users to switch the handset from one side of the head to the other during a conversation, to reduce the possibly harmful effects of microwaves emitted by the phone.
Hansson Mild, a specialist in electromagnetic fields, said the questionnaires circulated to 17,000 people built on the experiences of users in other countries who had reported similar complaints.

The dermatology unit of Sweden's world-famous Karolinska Institute said in June that "electro-hypersensitive" people appeared to suffer worse than other users of mobile phones, citing such complaints as skin and eye irritation and headaches.
